edits.definition: Speed is the rate at which an object covers distance — how much ground it covers in each unit of time. It is calculated as speed = distance ÷ time: a cyclist covering 30 kilometres in 2 hours rides at 15 km/h; a cheetah covering 100 metres in 4 seconds runs at 25 m/s. The SI unit is metre per second, and since most journeys speed up and slow down along the way, we usually quote the average speed — total distance divided by total time. Speed ignores direction entirely; it answers only 'how fast?', never 'which way?' — that fuller quantity, with direction included, is called velocity.

Revolution is the Earth's second great motion: its year-long journey around the Sun along a slightly oval (elliptical) orbit, at an average distance of about 150 million kilometres. One complete revolution takes about 365¼ days — the extra quarter-day is why the calendar adds a leap day every fourth year — and this circuit, combined with the fixed 23.5° tilt of the axis, produces the seasons: whichever hemisphere leans towards the Sun during its orbit receives longer days and more direct rays. While revolving, the Earth also spins on its axis, giving the day inside the year.

Metals meet air and moisture each with their own defence. Iron rusts readily, the flaky oxide crumbling away and exposing fresh metal — the worst outcome. Aluminium and copper react quickly at first but then form a thin, firm layer of oxide that clings tightly and shields the metal beneath — aluminium's dull coat is why it seems to resist 'rusting'. Gold and platinum barely react at all, staying bright through centuries — the reason rings and medals are made of them. So a metal's fate in air depends on the kind of layer its own reaction builds: protective, or flaking away.

Inequality and discrimination are two faces of unfairness. Inequality is the unequal distribution of what people need — wealth, land, schooling, healthcare, opportunity — so that whole groups start life's race metres behind others. Discrimination is unequal treatment based on identity: refusing someone work, entry, respect or justice because of their caste, gender, religion, language or disability, whether by open exclusion or quiet bias. The two feed each other — discrimination locks groups into inequality, and inequality makes discrimination easier to normalise — and the Constitution attacks both: Articles 14–16 guarantee equality and ban discrimination, and the state is directed to reduce inequality through welfare and reservation.

Ashoka changed Buddhism's history. After the Kalinga war's slaughter turned him to the Buddha's teaching (c. 261 BCE), he made the religion's spread a project of the state: he carved the Buddha's message on rock and pillar edicts across the subcontinent so all subjects could read of dhamma — kindness, truthfulness, tolerance; he built stupas enshrining relics, sent his own son Mahendra and daughter Sanghamitra to carry the teaching to Sri Lanka, and dispatched missionaries along the trade routes to Central Asia and Southeast Asia. Royal patronage gave a provincial sect roads, monuments and prestige — and Buddhism stepped onto the world stage.

The Bahmani Kingdom was the independent Muslim sultanate founded in the Deccan in 1347 by Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah after revolting against Delhi, with its capital later at Bidar. For nearly two centuries it contested the Vijayanagara empire across the Krishna–Tungabhadra doab in wars that shaped the southern peninsula. Its own story ended in fragmentation: around 1527 it broke into five successor sultanates — Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Berar, Bidar and Golconda — the Deccan Sultanates, which ruled the region until the Mughals absorbed them a century later. The Bahmanis left behind fine Indo-Persian architecture and the pattern of a divided, culturally rich Deccan.

The Battle of Plassey (23 June 1757) is the moment the East India Company stopped being a trading company and became a ruler. Robert Clive's forces met the much larger army of Siraj-ud-Daulah, the young Nawab of Bengal, near the Bhagirathi river — and won because the Nawab's commander Mir Jafar had been bribed into standing aside. The victory gave the Company the puppet Nawab it wanted and, after 1765, the diwani — the right to collect Bengal's revenues. With Bengal's taxes financing its armies, the Company's conquest of India had begun; Plassey is where the money for it was found.

The additive inverse of an integer is the number that cancels it to zero on addition: the additive inverse of 7 is −7, of −9 is 9, and of 0 is 0 itself — because a + (−a) = 0 for every integer. It is also called the opposite or the negation of the number, and on the number line it is the mirror point at the same distance from zero on the other side. Additive inverses are what make subtraction possible in integer arithmetic: a − b is defined as a plus the additive inverse of b, so every difference becomes an addition.

Word problems become equations through a fixed translation. Read the story to find what is unknown; give it a letter (the price of one notebook is x). Then restate each sentence as arithmetic: 'three notebooks cost ₹20 more than my ₹50' becomes 3x = 50 + 20, or however the relation truly reads. Solve the resulting linear equation by the balance method, and finish by answering the original question in words — not just x = 12, but 'each notebook costs ₹12'. The equation is only a machine for the sentence: if the translation is wrong, a perfectly solved equation still gives a wrong story.

A triangle is the closed figure formed by three straight sides joining three vertices, and it carries three interior angles whose sum is a fixed 180° — whatever the triangle's shape, the three angles fill exactly half a turn. That sum is the triangle's defining law: know any two angles and the third falls out by subtraction; find that two angles together exceed 90° and you know the triangle is obtuse without measuring. Triangles are classified by sides — equilateral, isosceles, scalene — and by angles — acute, right, obtuse — and every straight-sided figure in geometry can be cut into them.

Area is the size of the flat region enclosed by a closed figure — the 'amount of space' inside its boundary, counted in square units. It answers covering questions: how much carpet, how many tiles, how much paint. A shape holding eight 1 cm × 1 cm squares has area 8 cm²; rectangles multiply their two sides, triangles take half the base times height, and irregular figures are covered by counting whole and part squares on a grid. Area is always zero for a line and always stated in square units — figures with the same perimeter can enclose very different areas, and vice versa.

A number pattern is a list arranged by a rule the listmaker never states aloud: 2, 5, 8, 11 (add 3 each time); 1, 2, 4, 8 (double); 1, 1, 2, 3, 5 (add the previous two); 100, 92, 85 (no constant step — subtract 8, then 7). Pattern-reading is the search for that hidden rule by comparing consecutive terms: how do we get from each number to the next, and does the answer keep working? Once the rule is found, the pattern is mastered — the tenth or hundredth term can be written without building the ones between, because the rule generates the whole list.

Metals and non-metals split the periodic table's properties between them. Metals — iron, copper, aluminium, gold — are lustrous (shiny when polished), hard but malleable (beaten into sheets) and ductile (drawn into wires), and they are excellent conductors of both heat and electricity, which is why wires and pans are metal. Non-metals — sulphur, carbon, oxygen — are usually dull, brittle when solid, and poor conductors (insulators), with graphite the famous exception that conducts. The property list is the identification kit: shine, hardness, conduction on one side; dullness, brittleness, insulation on the other.

Changes divide into those that can be undone and those that cannot. A reversible change restores the original easily: ice freezes and melts back, steam condenses, a rubber band stretches and returns, salt dissolves and reappears on evaporation. An irreversible change is one-way: burnt paper is not paper again, milk once curdled stays curdled, a cut apple browns, bread bakes to bread for good. As a rule of thumb, most physical changes reverse while chemical changes do not — the new substance formed has no way back without another chemical reaction. Reversibility is the everyday test for asking which kind of change has happened.

Factors and multiples are the two directions of one multiplication fact. A factor of a number divides it exactly, leaving no remainder: 4 is a factor of 20 because 4 × 5 = 20. A multiple of a number is any product made by multiplying it by a whole number: 20, 40, 60 are multiples of 20, and also of each of its factors. So 20's factors are finite — 1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 20 — while its multiples run on forever. Every number is a factor and a multiple of itself, 1 is a factor of every number, and 0 is a multiple of everything but a factor of nothing.

Subtracting fractions finds the difference between two fractional parts, and its first requirement is a common unit: you can only take thirds from thirds. Like fractions subtract immediately (5/7 − 2/7 = 3/7 — five units minus two). Unlike fractions must first be rewritten with the LCM of the denominators as the common denominator — 3/4 − 1/6 becomes 9/12 − 2/12 = 7/12 — after which the numerators subtract over the shared base. Mixed numbers are handled by borrowing one whole as the necessary fractions, or by converting to improper fractions first. The answer is always reduced to lowest terms.

Perimeter is the distance all the way around a closed flat shape — the length of its boundary, as if you walked the edge exactly once. A square's perimeter is four times its side; a rectangle's is twice the sum of its length and breadth; any polygon's perimeter is the sum of its sides; a circle's perimeter is its circumference, 2πr. It is measured in plain length units (cm, m, km), not squares — perimeter runs along the boundary while area fills the region inside, and the two can change independently: a long thin rectangle can hold the same perimeter as a square with half the area.

Reflection is light's bounce: when a ray of light strikes a surface, part of it is thrown back — regularly and mirror-like from a smooth surface, scattered in all directions from a rough one. Seeing is reflection at work: most objects emit no light of their own; they reflect whatever falls on them, and the reflected rays enter our eyes and let the brain build the image of the object's shape and colour. The law of reflection governs the smooth case — the angle of bouncing equals the angle of arrival — and it is what makes mirrors, still water and polished metal act as pictures of the world.

Rusting is slow chemistry on iron: where iron, oxygen and moisture are present together, the metal combines with oxygen in the presence of water to form iron oxide — a reddish-brown, flaky coating we call rust. Rust does not protect: it crumbles off, exposing fresh iron, so given time the whole piece weakens and eats through. Rusting needs air and water together — iron kept dry, or under boiled water with no dissolved air, does not rust — which is why prevention works by keeping one of them away: paint, oil or grease, galvanising with zinc, and alloying into stainless steel.

Physical and chemical changes answer to one question: is anything new made? A physical change alters state, shape, size or appearance — ice melting, wire bending, salt dissolving — while the substance stays the same, and the change can usually be reversed. A chemical change produces entirely new substances with new properties — rust from iron, ash from paper, curd from milk — and does not undo itself by simple means. The reliable tests are the signs of chemistry: a new colour, a gas released, heat or light given out, a new solid settling. Where nothing new forms, the change was only physical.
